lessons.title: Upholstery Leather Production
lessons.body: Upholstery leather is thick, durable, and made for furniture, car seats, and bags. Start with hides from cattle or goats. For furniture, use full-grain hides at least 1.2â1.5 mm thick. After tanning (chrome or vegetable), you need to soften and finish the leather. For chrome-tanned upholstery, drum dye the leather to the desired colour, then fatliquor with 8â10% oil to keep it supple. Dry by hanging or vacuum drying to 12â14% moisture. Then staking (mechanical softening) is criticalârun the leather through a staking machine 2â3 times to break fibres and make it pliable. For a natural look, apply a light coat of clear lacquer or wax. For a matte finish, use a duller. In Africa, many workshops use vegetable-tanned goat leather for traditional chairs and poufs. Vegetable tanning takes longer (weeks) but gives a firm, earthy feel. After tanning, apply a mixture of neatsfoot oil and beeswax (50:50) to condition. For upholstery, thickness matters: 1.5â2 mm for heavy-use sofas, 1.0â1.2 mm for decorative cushions. You can also emboss patterns using heated brass platesâcommon in Moroccan leatherwork. Test your finish by folding the leather; it should not crack. Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sun. Market your upholstery leather to local furniture makersâa single hide (2â3 mÂ²) can cover a small armchair. Price: $30â$60 per hide depending on quality. With practice, you can produce 10â15 hides per week in a small workshop.

lessons.title: Garment and Glove Leather
lessons.body: Garment and glove leather must be soft, lightweight, and flexible. Use sheep, goat, or lamb skinsâthey are thin (0.5â0.8 mm) and have a fine grain. After tanning (usually chrome), the leather is shaved to uniform thickness on a splitting machine. Then it is dyed in a drum with acid dyes at 40â50Â°C for 1â2 hours. Rinse and fatliquor with 10â12% sulfated oil to keep it soft. Dry by hanging or toggle drying (stretched on frames) to prevent shrinkage. For glove leather, you need extreme softnessârun through a staking machine 3â4 times, then mill in a drum with wooden balls for 2â3 hours. This breaks the fibres without damaging the grain. For garment leather, a light spray finish of polyurethane or acrylic gives water resistance. In Africa, many tanneries in Nigeria and Ethiopia produce goat glove leather for local markets. A key test: fold the leather like a gloveâit should feel like cloth. For gloves, you need 0.4â0.6 mm thickness; for jackets, 0.7â0.9 mm. Dye penetration must be completeâcut a cross-section to check. Common defects are veiny grain or scars; select clean skins. After finishing, measure per square foot. A goat skin yields 4â6 sq ft. Price: $2â$4 per sq ft for garment, $3â$5 for glove. You can sell to tailors, glove makers, or export to Europe. Keep leather away from moisture; store flat with tissue paper between layers. For a small workshop, a drum, a splitting machine, and a staking machine are essential. Start with 20 skins per week.

lessons.title: Shoe Upper Leather
lessons.body: Shoe upper leather needs strength, breathability, and a good finish. Use cattle hide (full-grain or corrected-grain) at 1.2â1.4 mm thickness. After tanning (chrome or vegetable), the leather is sammed (moistened) and set out. For shoe uppers, you want a tight grain. Defects like scratches are sanded and buffed to create corrected grain, then embossed with a plate to mimic full grain. Dye in a drum with anionic dyes at 60Â°C for 1 hour. Fatliquor with 6â8% oilâtoo much oil weakens the leather. Dry by vacuum or hanging to 14% moisture. Then stake and buff. For a shiny finish, apply a base coat of polyurethane, then a top coat of nitrocellulose lacquer. For matte, use a wax finish. In Africa, Ethiopia and Nigeria have tanneries making shoe upper leather for local shoemakers. Test quality by flexing: 100,000 flexes without cracking is ideal. Also check water resistanceâdrop water on the surface; it should bead for at least 30 seconds. For safety shoes, use 1.5â1.8 mm thickness. For dress shoes, 1.0â1.2 mm. Cut patterns to minimise wasteâa hide of 20 sq ft makes 2â3 pairs of shoes. Price: $3â$6 per sq ft. Sell to shoe factories or artisan cobblers. Store in rolls, not folded, to avoid creases. With a drum, splitting machine, and spray booth, you can produce 50â100 sq ft per day.

lessons.title: Belting and Strap Leather
lessons.body: Belting and strap leather must be strong, stretch-resistant, and thick. Use cattle hide (bull or ox) at 3â5 mm thickness. Vegetable tanning is preferred because it gives a firm, dense leather that holds shape. After tanning, the hide is split to the required thickness, then shaved. For belts, you need 3â4 mm; for heavy machinery belting, 5â6 mm. The leather is then wetted and stretched on a frame to remove wrinkles. Drying takes 2â3 days in shade. Do not use heatâit makes leather brittle. After drying, apply a mixture of tallow and cod oil (70:30) to lubricate fibres. Then compress the leather with a roller or hammer to increase density. For straps, cut strips 2â5 cm wide, bevel edges, and burnish with a slicker and water. Dye with oil-based dye for deep penetration. In Africa, many artisans make belts from vegetable-tanned goat or cow leather. For machinery belting, you need to join ends with a lap splice and rivets or stitching. Test tensile strength: a 2 cm wide strap should hold at least 200 kg without breaking. For horse harness, use 4â5 mm thickness. Price: $5â$10 per sq ft for belting, $2â$4 per sq ft for belt strips. Sell to farmers, factories, or leather crafters. Store flat, away from moisture. A small workshop can produce 10â20 belts per day with a splitting machine, strap cutter, and burnisher.

lessons.title: Bookbinding and Craft Leather
lessons.body: Bookbinding and craft leather is thin, flexible, and takes tooling well. Use goat, calf, or sheep skin at 0.5â0.8 mm thickness. Vegetable-tanned leather is best because it accepts dyes, gold tooling, and embossing. After tanning, the leather is split to uniform thickness, then dyed with spirit or water-based dyes. For bookbinding, you want a smooth grainâskive edges thin for turning in. Apply a paste of wheat starch and water to the flesh side to stiffen it slightly. Dry under pressure between boards to keep flat. For craft leather (wallets, purses), you can use chrome-tanned leather for softness, but vegetable-tanned is preferred for tooling. To tool, case the leather (dampen with sponge), then stamp with heated brass tools. In Africa, Moroccan and Nigerian craftsmen are famous for leather bookbinding and poufs. For a book cover, cut leather 1 cm larger than the book board. Glue with PVA, then turn edges and press. For decoration, use gold leaf with heated tools. Test flexibility: fold the leather 180Â°âit should not crack. Price: $4â$8 per sq ft for bookbinding leather, $2â$5 for craft. Sell to bookbinders, craft shops, or tourists. Store in a cool, dark place. With a skiving machine, press, and tooling set, you can produce 20â30 book covers per week.

lessons.title: Specialty Leathers
lessons.body: Specialty leathers are made for specific functions: waterproof, fire-resistant, or decorative. Examples include patent leather (high-gloss), nubuck (brushed grain), suede (flesh side), and exotic leathers (ostrich, crocodile). For patent leather, start with a corrected-grain hide, apply a base coat of polyurethane, then a top coat of acrylic lacquer, and cure under UV light. The finish must be mirror-like. For nubuck, buff the grain side with fine sandpaper (400 grit) to raise a velvet nap. For suede, use the flesh sideâsplit the hide, then buff. In Africa, ostrich leather from South Africa is a luxury export. Ostrich skin has quill follicles that create a unique bumpy texture. Tan with chrome, then dye and finish with a light wax. Crocodile leather from Nile crocodiles is also prized. For these, you must comply with CITES regulations. Other specialty leathers include: fire-resistant leather (treated with ammonium phosphate), used for welding aprons; and waterproof leather (silicone or wax treatment). For a small workshop, focus on nubuck and suedeâthey are easier. Use a buffing machine with 180â400 grit. Dye with a spray gun for even colour. Test waterproofing by dropping waterâit should roll off. Price: patent $8â$15 per sq ft, nubuck $5â$8, ostrich $20â$40. Sell to fashion designers, shoe makers, or export. Store specialty leathers in acid-free paper. With a spray booth and buffing machine, you can produce 50 sq ft per day.

quiz.q: What is the ideal thickness for upholstery leather used on heavy-use sofas?
quiz.explanation: Heavy-use sofas require thicker leather (1.5â2.0 mm) for durability.

quiz.q: Which tanning method is preferred for upholstery leather that needs a firm, earthy feel?
quiz.explanation: Vegetable tanning gives a firm, earthy feel suitable for traditional upholstery.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of staking in upholstery leather production?
options: B) To soften the leather by breaking fibres
quiz.explanation: Staking mechanically softens leather by breaking fibres to make it pliable.

quiz.q: Which animal skin is commonly used for garment and glove leather due to its thinness?
quiz.explanation: Sheep and goat skins are thin and fine-grained, ideal for garments and gloves.

quiz.q: What is the typical thickness range for glove leather?
quiz.explanation: Glove leather is very thin, usually 0.4â0.6 mm, for flexibility.

quiz.q: Which process is used to make glove leather extremely soft?
options: B) Staking and milling with wooden balls
quiz.explanation: Staking and milling with wooden balls break fibres to achieve extreme softness.

quiz.q: What is a common test for garment leather quality?
options: A) Fold it like a glove; it should feel like cloth
B) Drop water on it; it should bead
C) Stretch it to 200% without breaking
D) Burn it to check fire resistance
quiz.explanation: Garment leather should be soft and flexible, feeling like cloth when folded.

quiz.q: What thickness is recommended for shoe upper leather for dress shoes?
quiz.explanation: Dress shoes typically use 1.0â1.2 mm thick leather for a balance of strength and elegance.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of fatliquoring in shoe upper leather production?
options: B) To soften and lubricate the leather
quiz.explanation: Fatliquoring lubricates fibres to keep leather soft and prevent cracking.

quiz.q: How many flexes should shoe upper leather withstand without cracking?
quiz.explanation: Good shoe upper leather should withstand 100,000 flexes without cracking.

quiz.q: Which tanning method is preferred for belting leather?
quiz.explanation: Vegetable tanning gives firm, dense leather that holds shape, ideal for belts.

quiz.q: What thickness is typical for heavy machinery belting leather?
quiz.explanation: Heavy machinery belting requires thick leather, usually 5â6 mm.

quiz.q: What mixture is applied to belting leather after drying to lubricate fibres?
quiz.explanation: A mixture of tallow and cod oil (70:30) is used to lubricate belting leather.

quiz.q: What is the minimum tensile strength for a 2 cm wide belt strap?
quiz.explanation: A 2 cm wide strap should hold at least 200 kg without breaking.

quiz.q: Which leather is best for bookbinding because it accepts tooling well?
quiz.explanation: Vegetable-tanned leather accepts dyes, gold tooling, and embossing well.

quiz.q: What thickness is typical for bookbinding leather?
quiz.explanation: Bookbinding leather is thin, usually 0.5â0.8 mm, for flexibility.

quiz.q: What is 'casing' in leather tooling?
options: B) Dampening the leather with a sponge
quiz.explanation: Casing is dampening leather with a sponge to prepare it for tooling.

quiz.q: Which African country is famous for ostrich leather?
quiz.explanation: South Africa is a leading producer of ostrich leather.

quiz.q: What unique feature does ostrich leather have?
options: B) Quill follicles creating a bumpy texture
quiz.explanation: Ostrich leather has quill follicles that create a distinctive bumpy texture.

quiz.q: What is nubuck?
options: A) Leather with a high-gloss finish
B) Leather buffed on the grain side to raise a nap
C) Leather from the flesh side
D) Leather treated for fire resistance
quiz.explanation: Nubuck is leather buffed on the grain side to create a velvet-like nap.

quiz.q: Which chemical is used to make fire-resistant leather?
quiz.explanation: Ammonium phosphate is used to treat leather for fire resistance.

quiz.q: What is the price range for patent leather per square foot?
quiz.explanation: Patent leather typically sells for $8â$15 per square foot.

quiz.q: Which tool is essential for making belts from strap leather?
quiz.explanation: A strap cutter is used to cut uniform strips for belts.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for upholstery leather after drying?
quiz.explanation: Upholstery leather is dried to 12â14% moisture content for optimal properties.

quiz.q: Which dyeing method is used for garment leather in a drum?
quiz.explanation: Garment leather is typically drum-dyed with acid dyes at 40â50Â°C.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a splitting machine in leather production?
options: B) To shave leather to uniform thickness
quiz.explanation: A splitting machine shaves leather to a uniform thickness.

quiz.q: Which leather type is made from the flesh side of the hide?
quiz.explanation: Suede is made from the flesh side of the hide, buffed to a nap.

quiz.q: What is a key quality test for belting leather?
quiz.explanation: Belting leather must have high tensile strength to withstand pulling.

quiz.q: Which African country is known for leather bookbinding and poufs?
quiz.explanation: Morocco is famous for leather bookbinding and poufs.

quiz.q: What is the typical price per square foot for ostrich leather?
quiz.explanation: Ostrich leather is a luxury product, priced at $20â$40 per square foot.
